name: Barbell Back Squat (High Bar)
instructions: Position the bar high on your traps, feet roughly shoulder-width apart.
Brace your core and squat down by bending the knees and hips until thighs are at least parallel to the floor.
Drive through the floor to stand back up to the starting position.
coachNote: The high bar position keeps the torso more upright than a low bar squat, placing more direct emphasis on the quads.
tips: Keep the chest up and knees tracking over the toes.
Descend at a controlled pace and drive up with intent.
commonMistakes: Letting the knees cave inward.
Rounding the lower back at the bottom of the squat.
benefits: Foundational compound lift for lower-body strength and mass.
Trains the quads, glutes, and core together.
safetyNotes: Use a rack with safety pins set to an appropriate height.
Learn the pattern with lighter weight before loading heavy.
startingPosition: Standing, bar on the upper traps, feet shoulder-width.
endingPosition: Thighs at or below parallel, then returned to standing.

name: Barbell Back Squat (Low Bar)
instructions: Position the bar lower across the rear delts, feet slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Hinge slightly more at the hips as you descend, keeping the torso leaned forward compared to a high bar squat.
Drive through the floor to stand back up to the starting position.
coachNote: The low bar position shifts more emphasis onto the hips and posterior chain, often allowing heavier total loads.
tips: Keep the bar path vertical over mid-foot.
Brace hard before each descent.
commonMistakes: Letting the bar drift forward over the toes.
Losing the forward torso lean too early on the ascent.
benefits: Allows heavier loading than a high bar squat for many lifters.
Popular among powerlifters for maximal strength.
safetyNotes: Use a rack with safety pins.
Master the high bar squat pattern first if new to squatting.
startingPosition: Standing, bar across the rear delts, feet wider than shoulder-width.
endingPosition: Thighs at or below parallel, then returned to standing.

name: Front Squat
instructions: Rest the bar across the front of the shoulders, elbows raised high, gripping the bar with fingertips.
Squat down keeping the torso as upright as possible.
Drive through the floor to stand back up.
coachNote: Keeping the elbows up is essential — as they drop, the bar loses support and the torso tends to collapse forward.
tips: Keep the elbows pointed forward and high throughout.
Brace the core hard to stay upright.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows drop, causing the bar to roll forward.
Excessive forward lean.
benefits: Very upright torso position emphasizes the quads heavily.
Builds core and upper back strength to support the bar.
safetyNotes: Use a rack with safety pins.
Learn the front rack position with light weight first.
startingPosition: Standing, bar racked across the front shoulders, elbows high.
endingPosition: Thighs at or below parallel, then returned to standing.

name: Goblet Squat
instructions: Hold a dumbbell or kettlebell vertically against your chest with both hands.
Squat down between your knees, keeping the torso upright.
Drive through the floor to stand back up.
coachNote: One of the best squat patterns for beginners since holding the weight in front naturally encourages an upright torso.
tips: Keep the elbows pointed down between the knees at the bottom.
Keep the weight close to the chest throughout.
commonMistakes: Letting the weight drift away from the chest.
Rounding the upper back.
benefits: Beginner-friendly squat pattern.
Teaches proper squat depth and torso position.
safetyNotes: Use a weight you can control through the full range.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Standing, weight held vertically at the chest.
endingPosition: Squatted down with thighs at or below parallel.

name: Zercher Squat
instructions: Hold the bar in the crooks of your elbows, arms wrapped around it, standing tall.
Squat down keeping the torso as upright as possible.
Drive through the floor to stand back up.
coachNote: This front-loaded position forces a very upright torso and heavily challenges core bracing.
tips: Pad the bar or wear long sleeves to reduce discomfort on the elbows.
Keep the core braced hard throughout.
commonMistakes: Letting the torso collapse forward.
Using too much weight before the elbow crease adapts.
benefits: Strong core and upper back demand alongside quad training.
Unique loading position for variety.
safetyNotes: Start light to adapt to the uncomfortable bar position.
Use a rack with safety pins.
startingPosition: Standing, bar held in the crooks of the elbows.
endingPosition: Thighs at or below parallel, then returned to standing.

name: Box Squat
instructions: Set up a box or bench at or slightly below squat depth behind you, bar on your back.
Squat down until you lightly touch the box, keeping tension in the legs.
Drive back up to standing without bouncing off the box.
coachNote: Sitting back to the box teaches a strong hip-hinge pattern and removes any stretch-reflex bounce out of the bottom.
tips: Touch the box lightly, don't fully relax onto it.
Keep the shins relatively vertical as you sit back.
commonMistakes: Fully relaxing onto the box, losing tension.
Bouncing off the box using momentum.
benefits: Teaches a controlled, powerful squat pattern.
Useful for pinpointing consistent squat depth.
safetyNotes: Use a stable, secure box or bench.
Start with lighter weight to learn the touch-and-go technique.
startingPosition: Standing, bar on the back, box positioned behind.
endingPosition: Seated lightly on the box, then returned to standing.

name: Pause Squat
instructions: Set up and descend into a squat as normal.
Pause for 2-3 seconds at the bottom position, maintaining tension and a braced core.
Drive through the floor to stand back up.
coachNote: Removing the stretch-reflex bounce out of the bottom builds significant raw strength and exposes technique weaknesses.
tips: Stay tight and braced throughout the entire pause.
Use a lighter weight than your regular squat to start.
commonMistakes: Relaxing during the pause, losing tension.
Rushing the pause instead of holding the full duration.
benefits: Builds strength out of the bottom position.
Removes momentum, exposing and fixing technique flaws.
safetyNotes: Use a rack with safety pins.
Reduce the load compared to your regular squat.
startingPosition: Standing, bar on the back.
endingPosition: Paused at the bottom of the squat, then returned to standing.

name: Smith Machine Squat
instructions: Position yourself under the Smith machine bar with feet slightly forward of your hips.
Unrack the bar and squat down, keeping the torso upright.
Drive through the floor to stand back up.
coachNote: The fixed bar path allows safe training near failure without a spotter, but stepping the feet slightly forward is important to match the vertical bar path.
tips: Position the feet slightly ahead of the hips to match the fixed bar path.
Keep the core braced throughout.
commonMistakes: Standing directly under the bar as in a free squat, causing an unnatural path.
Locking the bar before fully descending.
benefits: Allows safe near-failure training.
Fixed path reduces stabilization demand for beginners.
safetyNotes: Confirm the safety hooks are set correctly.
Ensure the bar is unlocked before descending.
startingPosition: Standing, bar racked on the Smith machine, feet slightly forward.
endingPosition: Thighs at or below parallel, then returned to standing.

name: Hack Squat (Machine)
instructions: Position your shoulders and back against the pads of the hack squat machine, feet on the platform.
Release the safety handles and squat down by bending the knees.
Drive through the platform to extend the legs back to the starting position.
coachNote: The fixed, angled path allows very heavy quad-focused loading with minimal balance demand.
tips: Keep the lower back pressed against the pad throughout.
Avoid letting the knees cave inward.
commonMistakes: Going too deep and rounding the lower back off the pad.
Using too much weight and shortening the range of motion.
benefits: Allows very heavy quad-focused loading safely.
Minimal balance demand compared to free-weight squats.
safetyNotes: Use the safety handles to lock the machine before adjusting foot position.
Avoid excessive depth that lifts the lower back off the pad.
startingPosition: Shoulders against the pads, legs extended.
endingPosition: Knees bent, thighs near the chest.

name: Belt Squat
instructions: Attach a belt squat harness around your hips and stand on the raised platforms.
Squat down by bending the hips and knees, keeping the torso upright.
Drive through the platform to stand back up.
coachNote: Since the load hangs from the hips rather than the spine, this is an excellent option for lifters wanting to train legs hard without any spinal loading.
tips: Keep the torso upright throughout.
Control the descent rather than dropping quickly.
commonMistakes: Leaning too far forward.
Using momentum instead of a controlled squat.
benefits: Removes spinal loading, ideal for lifters managing back issues.
Allows heavy quad and glute training safely.
safetyNotes: Ensure the harness is secured properly before loading.
Use the platform safety stops as needed.
startingPosition: Standing on the platforms, harness loaded at the hips.
endingPosition: Thighs at or below parallel, then returned to standing.

name: Landmine Squat
instructions: Hold the loaded end of a landmine-anchored barbell at chest height with both hands.
Squat down keeping the torso upright, the bar's arc naturally guiding your path.
Drive through the floor to stand back up.
coachNote: The landmine's arcing path is very forgiving and beginner-friendly compared to a straight barbell squat.
tips: Keep the bar close to the chest throughout.
Keep the torso upright and core braced.
commonMistakes: Letting the bar drift away from the chest.
Rounding the upper back.
benefits: Beginner-friendly squat pattern.
Minimal setup required beyond a barbell and anchor.
safetyNotes: Secure the barbell end firmly in the landmine attachment.
Start light to learn the pattern.
startingPosition: Standing, bar held at the chest.
endingPosition: Thighs at or below parallel, then returned to standing.

name: Overhead Squat
instructions: Hold a barbell locked out overhead with a wide grip, standing tall.
Squat down while keeping the bar directly overhead and the torso upright.
Drive through the floor to stand back up, maintaining the overhead lockout throughout.
coachNote: This demands excellent shoulder, hip, and ankle mobility — use very light weight until the pattern is well-grooved.
tips: Keep the bar directly over mid-foot throughout.
Brace the core hard to keep the torso upright.
commonMistakes: Letting the bar drift forward.
Attempting heavy loads before mastering the mobility requirements.
benefits: Builds full-body mobility, stability, and strength together.
Common assessment and training tool in Olympic weightlifting.
safetyNotes: Start with an empty bar or PVC pipe to learn the pattern.
Stop if the bar drifts forward significantly.
startingPosition: Standing, bar locked out overhead.
endingPosition: Thighs at or below parallel, bar still locked out overhead.

name: Trap Bar Deadlift
instructions: Stand inside a loaded trap bar, gripping the neutral handles.
Squat down to grip the handles with a flat back and upright torso.
Drive through the floor to stand up, extending the hips and knees together.
coachNote: The trap bar's centered load and more upright torso make this significantly more quad-dominant than a conventional deadlift.
tips: Keep the chest up and shins vertical at the start.
Drive through the whole foot as you stand.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips shoot up faster than the chest.
Rounding the lower back.
benefits: More beginner-friendly than a conventional deadlift.
Trains the quads more directly than a straight bar deadlift.
safetyNotes: Learn the pattern with light weight first.
Keep the back flat throughout the lift.
startingPosition: Standing inside the trap bar, gripping the handles, flat back.
endingPosition: Standing tall, hips fully extended.

name: Bulgarian Split Squat
instructions: Stand a couple feet in front of a bench, resting the top of one foot on it behind you.
Lower your body by bending the front knee until the back knee nearly touches the floor.
Drive through the front foot to return to standing.
coachNote: A brutal single-leg quad and glute builder — expect significant balance demand at first.
tips: Keep most of your weight on the front leg.
Keep the torso upright throughout the movement.
commonMistakes: Letting the front knee cave inward.
Placing the rear foot too close, limiting range of motion.
benefits: Strong unilateral quad and glute builder.
Addresses left-right strength imbalances.
safetyNotes: Use a stable bench and secure footing.
Start with bodyweight to learn the balance before adding load.
startingPosition: Standing, rear foot elevated on a bench behind you.
endingPosition: Front knee bent, rear knee near the floor.

name: Smith Machine Bulgarian Split Squat
instructions: Position the Smith machine bar across your upper back, with the rear foot elevated on a bench behind you.
Lower your body by bending the front knee until the back knee nearly touches the floor.
Drive through the front foot to return to standing.
coachNote: The fixed bar path removes the balance challenge of a dumbbell version, letting you focus purely on loading the legs.
tips: Keep most of your weight on the front leg.
Position your feet to match the fixed vertical bar path.
commonMistakes: Letting the front knee cave inward.
Standing too far under the bar for the fixed path.
benefits: Removes balance demand for heavier loading.
Strong unilateral quad and glute builder.
safetyNotes: Use a stable bench and secure footing.
Confirm the bar is unlocked before descending.
startingPosition: Bar on the back, rear foot elevated on a bench behind you.
endingPosition: Front knee bent, rear knee near the floor.

name: Split Squat (Static Lunge)
instructions: Stand in a staggered stance with one foot forward and one back, holding dumbbells at your sides.
Lower your body by bending both knees until the back knee nearly touches the floor.
Drive through the front foot to return to standing.
coachNote: A great entry point into unilateral leg training before progressing to the more demanding Bulgarian split squat.
tips: Keep the torso upright throughout.
Keep most of the weight on the front leg.
commonMistakes: Letting the front knee cave inward.
Taking too short a stance, limiting range of motion.
benefits: Beginner-friendly unilateral leg exercise.
Addresses left-right strength imbalances.
safetyNotes: Use a stance length that allows a full range of motion.
Start with bodyweight before adding load.
startingPosition: Staggered stance, one foot forward, one back.
endingPosition: Front knee bent, rear knee near the floor.

name: Walking Lunge (Dumbbell)
instructions: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Step forward into a lunge, lowering the back knee toward the floor.
Drive through the front foot to step forward into the next lunge, alternating legs.
coachNote: The continuous forward movement adds a dynamic, functional component compared to a static split squat.
tips: Keep the torso upright throughout each step.
Take a stride length that allows a 90-degree front knee bend.
commonMistakes: Taking too short a stride, limiting range of motion.
Letting the front knee cave inward.
benefits: Builds unilateral leg strength with a functional walking pattern.
Good for lower-body endurance and hypertrophy.
safetyNotes: Ensure adequate space to walk forward.
Start with bodyweight before adding load.
startingPosition: Standing, dumbbells at the sides.
endingPosition: Alternating lunges while walking forward.

name: Barbell Walking Lunge
instructions: Stand with a barbell racked across your upper back.
Step forward into a lunge, lowering the back knee toward the floor.
Drive through the front foot to step forward into the next lunge, alternating legs.
coachNote: Having the bar on the back frees the hands, but demands more core and balance control than the dumbbell version.
tips: Keep the torso upright throughout each step.
Brace the core to maintain balance with the bar.
commonMistakes: Taking too short a stride.
Letting the torso lean forward excessively.
benefits: Allows heavier total loading than dumbbell lunges.
Builds unilateral leg strength and core stability.
safetyNotes: Ensure adequate space to walk forward safely.
Master the dumbbell version before progressing to the bar.
startingPosition: Standing, bar racked across the upper back.
endingPosition: Alternating lunges while walking forward.

name: Reverse Lunge
instructions: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Step backward into a lunge, lowering the back knee toward the floor.
Drive through the front foot to return to the starting position, then repeat on the other side.
coachNote: Stepping backward is generally easier on the knees than a forward lunge, making it a good starting point for beginners.
tips: Keep the torso upright throughout.
Keep most of the weight on the front leg.
commonMistakes: Letting the front knee cave inward.
Taking too short a step, limiting range of motion.
benefits: Knee-friendly unilateral leg exercise.
Good starting point for lunge pattern beginners.
safetyNotes: Start with bodyweight before adding load.
Keep a stable, controlled stepping motion.
startingPosition: Standing, dumbbells at the sides.
endingPosition: Back knee near the floor, front knee bent.

name: Forward Lunge
instructions: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Step forward into a lunge, lowering the back knee toward the floor.
Drive through the front foot to push back to the starting position, then repeat on the other side.
coachNote: Stepping forward and returning to the start (rather than continuing to walk) makes this easier to control in a confined space.
tips: Keep the torso upright throughout.
Push back through the front heel to return to start.
commonMistakes: Letting the front knee cave inward.
Leaning the torso too far forward.
benefits: Builds unilateral leg strength and stability.
Doesn't require walking space, unlike a walking lunge.
safetyNotes: Start with bodyweight before adding load.
Keep a stable, controlled stepping motion.
startingPosition: Standing, dumbbells at the sides.
endingPosition: Front knee bent, back knee near the floor.

name: Deficit Reverse Lunge
instructions: Stand on a low box or plate with a dumbbell in each hand.
Step backward and down into a reverse lunge, increasing the range of motion beyond a standard lunge.
Drive through the front foot to return to standing on the elevated surface.
coachNote: Elevating the front foot increases the range of motion, adding a stronger stretch stimulus to the front leg's quads and glutes.
tips: Use a stable, secure elevated surface.
Keep the torso upright throughout.
commonMistakes: Using an elevation too high before building adequate mobility.
Losing balance on the elevated surface.
benefits: Increases range of motion for greater hypertrophy stimulus.
Advanced progression from a standard reverse lunge.
safetyNotes: Use a stable platform.
Start with a small deficit height and progress gradually.
startingPosition: Standing on an elevated surface, dumbbells at the sides.
endingPosition: Back knee near the floor, front knee bent, standing on the elevated surface.

name: Cyclist Squat (Heel-Elevated)
instructions: Stand with your heels elevated on a small plate or wedge, feet close together, bar on your back.
Squat down keeping the torso very upright, knees traveling forward over the toes.
Drive through the floor to stand back up.
coachNote: Elevating the heels and using a narrow stance maximizes knee flexion and quad recruitment, minimizing glute and hamstring involvement.
tips: Keep the torso as upright as possible throughout.
Allow the knees to travel forward naturally.
commonMistakes: Using a stance too wide, reducing the intended quad emphasis.
Leaning the torso forward.
benefits: Maximizes quad recruitment.
Popular with bodybuilders seeking maximal quad development.
safetyNotes: Use a stable heel wedge or plates.
Start light to adapt to the demanding knee flexion range.
startingPosition: Standing, heels elevated, feet close together, bar on the back.
endingPosition: Deep knee flexion, torso upright, then returned to standing.

name: Spanish Squat (Band)
instructions: Anchor a thick resistance band around a sturdy post at knee height, looping it behind both knees.
Lean back against the band tension and squat down, keeping the shins vertical.
Drive back up to standing, using the band to help support the movement.
coachNote: This is a favorite rehab and prehab tool for building quad strength with minimal knee shear force, popular for managing patellar tendon issues.
tips: Keep the shins as vertical as possible throughout.
Lean back into the band for support and balance.
commonMistakes: Letting the knees travel too far forward.
Using a band too weak to provide adequate support.
benefits: Very knee-friendly quad exercise.
Popular tool for patellar tendon rehab and prehab.
safetyNotes: Ensure the band anchor is secure.
Use a band strength appropriate for your body weight.
startingPosition: Leaning back against the band, knees bent, shins vertical.
endingPosition: Standing tall, band tension maintained.

name: Sissy Squat
instructions: Stand holding onto a stable support, rising onto your toes.
Lean back and bend the knees, lowering your torso toward the floor in a straight line from knees to head.
Reverse the motion by extending the knees to return to standing.
coachNote: An intense, deep quad stretch and contraction exercise — start with a small range of motion and build up gradually.
tips: Hold onto a stable support throughout for balance.
Keep the hips extended, bending only at the knees.
commonMistakes: Bending at the hips instead of keeping a straight knees-to-head line.
Going too deep before building adequate strength.
benefits: Intense quad stretch and contraction.
No equipment needed beyond something to hold onto.
safetyNotes: Build up range of motion gradually.
Use a support for balance until confident.
startingPosition: Standing on toes, holding a support.
endingPosition: Torso and thighs in a straight line, leaned back with knees bent.

name: Sissy Squat Machine
instructions: Secure your ankles under the pads of the sissy squat machine, standing tall.
Lean back and bend the knees, lowering your torso in a straight line.
Reverse the motion by extending the knees to return to standing.
coachNote: The machine's ankle support and handles make this deep quad stretch far more accessible than the bodyweight version.
tips: Keep the hips extended, bending only at the knees.
Control the descent and ascent throughout.
commonMistakes: Bending at the hips instead of the knees.
Going too deep before building adequate strength.
benefits: More accessible than the bodyweight sissy squat.
Intense, isolated quad stretch and contraction.
safetyNotes: Secure the ankles properly before starting.
Build up range of motion gradually.
startingPosition: Standing, ankles secured, machine handles held.
endingPosition: Torso and thighs in a straight line, leaned back with knees bent.

name: Pistol Squat
instructions: Stand on one leg with the other leg extended straight in front of you.
Squat down on the standing leg as low as possible, keeping the extended leg off the floor.
Drive through the standing leg to return to standing.
coachNote: A demanding test of single-leg strength, balance, and ankle/hip mobility — build up through assisted progressions first.
tips: Use a support or counterbalance while learning.
Keep the extended leg as straight as possible throughout.
commonMistakes: Losing balance and falling backward.
Attempting this before building adequate single-leg strength.
benefits: Builds exceptional single-leg strength, balance, and mobility.
No equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Build up through easier single-leg progressions first.
Practice near a support or soft landing surface.
startingPosition: Standing on one leg, other leg extended forward.
endingPosition: Squatted low on the standing leg, other leg still extended.

name: Shrimp Squat
instructions: Stand on one leg, holding the other foot behind you with the same-side hand.
Squat down on the standing leg until the back knee nearly touches the floor.
Drive through the standing leg to return to standing.
coachNote: An even more advanced single-leg squat variation than the pistol squat, demanding significant quad strength and hip mobility.
tips: Use a support nearby while learning.
Keep the torso as upright as possible.
commonMistakes: Losing balance and touching down with the rear foot.
Attempting this before building strength with easier progressions.
benefits: Builds exceptional single-leg strength and control.
No equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Build up through easier single-leg progressions first.
Practice near a support surface.
startingPosition: Standing on one leg, other foot held behind by the same-side hand.
endingPosition: Squatted low on the standing leg, rear knee near the floor.

name: Skater Squat
instructions: Stand on one leg, extending the other leg behind you slightly bent.
Squat down on the standing leg, allowing the rear knee to lightly tap the floor behind you.
Drive through the standing leg to return to standing.
coachNote: A more accessible single-leg squat progression than a pistol squat since the rear leg doesn't need to stay fully extended.
tips: Use a support nearby while learning balance.
Let the rear knee tap lightly rather than absorbing weight.
commonMistakes: Letting the rear knee slam into the floor.
Leaning too far forward, losing balance.
benefits: More accessible progression toward a pistol squat.
Builds single-leg strength and balance.
safetyNotes: Use a soft surface or mat for the rear knee.
Practice near a support while learning.
startingPosition: Standing on one leg, other leg extended behind, slightly bent.
endingPosition: Squatted on the standing leg, rear knee lightly tapping the floor.

name: Box Step-Up
instructions: Stand facing a sturdy box or bench, holding dumbbells at your sides.
Step up onto the box with one foot, driving through that leg to bring the other foot up.
Step back down with control and repeat, alternating or completing all reps on one side first.
coachNote: Drive through the working leg on the box rather than pushing off the trailing foot to maximize the training effect.
tips: Place the whole foot on the box, not just the toes.
Avoid pushing off the back foot to help the movement.
commonMistakes: Using momentum from the trailing leg.
Using a box too high before building adequate strength.
benefits: Builds unilateral leg strength and functional stepping power.
Simple to scale by adjusting box height.
safetyNotes: Use a sturdy, stable box.
Choose a height that allows a controlled step without excessive knee strain.
startingPosition: Standing in front of the box, dumbbells at the sides.
endingPosition: Standing fully on top of the box.

name: Dumbbell Step-Up
instructions: Stand facing a bench, holding a dumbbell in each hand.
Step up onto the bench with one foot, driving through that leg.
Step back down with control and repeat on the same or alternating side.
coachNote: A staple bodybuilding step-up variation using a standard flat bench rather than a specialized box.
tips: Drive through the working leg, not the trailing foot.
Keep the torso upright throughout.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to help step up.
Placing only the toes on the bench instead of the full foot.
benefits: Builds unilateral leg strength using common gym equipment.
Simple to progressively overload.
safetyNotes: Use a stable, secure bench.
Choose a height appropriate to your mobility and strength.
startingPosition: Standing in front of the bench, dumbbells at the sides.
endingPosition: Standing fully on top of the bench.

name: Leg Press (45-Degree)
instructions: Sit in the leg press machine with feet shoulder-width apart on the platform.
Release the safety and lower the platform by bending the knees toward your chest.
Press through the platform to extend the legs back to the starting position without locking out the knees.
coachNote: A safe, guided way to load the quads heavily without the balance and spinal loading demands of a barbell squat.
tips: Avoid locking out the knees completely at the top.
Keep the lower back pressed against the pad.
commonMistakes: Letting the lower back round off the pad at the bottom.
Locking the knees out aggressively at the top.
benefits: Allows heavy quad loading with minimal balance demand.
Adjustable foot position for varied emphasis.
safetyNotes: Use the safety catches when loading or unloading the machine.
Avoid excessive depth that lifts the lower back off the pad.
startingPosition: Knees bent, platform lowered toward the chest.
endingPosition: Legs extended, knees not locked out.

name: Single-Leg Leg Press
instructions: Sit in the leg press machine and place one foot centered on the platform.
Lower the platform by bending the knee toward your chest.
Press through the platform to extend the leg, then complete reps before switching sides.
coachNote: Training one leg at a time on the leg press addresses imbalances that a bilateral press can mask.
tips: Center the foot on the platform for balanced pressing.
Use a lighter weight than your bilateral press.
commonMistakes: Letting the knee cave inward under the single-leg load.
Using too much weight and losing control.
benefits: Addresses left-right strength imbalances.
Builds strong single-leg quad strength.
safetyNotes: Use the safety catches when loading or unloading.
Start with a lighter weight than the bilateral version.
startingPosition: One foot on the platform, knee bent toward the chest.
endingPosition: Leg extended, knee not locked out.

name: Vertical Leg Press
instructions: Lie on your back under the vertical leg press machine, feet on the platform above you.
Lower the platform by bending the knees toward your chest.
Press through the platform to extend the legs back to the starting position.
coachNote: The vertical angle increases the demand on the quads through a deeper range of motion compared to a 45-degree press.
tips: Keep the lower back flat against the pad.
Avoid locking the knees out aggressively at the top.
commonMistakes: Letting the lower back round at the bottom.
Using too much weight and shortening the range.
benefits: Deeper range of motion than a 45-degree leg press.
Strong quad and glute stimulus.
safetyNotes: Use the safety catches when loading or unloading.
Avoid excessive depth that lifts the lower back off the pad.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, knees bent toward the chest, feet on the platform.
endingPosition: Legs extended, knees not locked out.

name: Leg Extension
instructions: Sit in the leg extension machine with the pad resting against your shins, knees bent.
Extend your legs by straightening the knees until fully extended.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: A pure quad isolation exercise, useful for finishing off a leg session or pre-fatiguing the quads before compound work.
tips: Squeeze the quads hard at the top of each rep.
Control the descent rather than letting the weight drop.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to swing the weight up.
Locking the knees out aggressively at the top.
benefits: Pure quad isolation without other muscle group involvement.
Easy to progressively overload.
safetyNotes: Adjust the seat and pad position correctly before loading.
Avoid excessive weight that strains the knee joint.
startingPosition: Knees bent, pad against the shins.
endingPosition: Legs fully extended.

name: Single-Leg Leg Extension
instructions: Sit in the leg extension machine with the pad resting against one shin, knee bent.
Extend that leg by straightening the knee until fully extended.
Lower with control, then complete reps before switching sides.
coachNote: Training one leg at a time allows a stronger mind-muscle connection and helps correct imbalances.
tips: Squeeze the quad hard at the top of each rep.
Control the descent rather than letting the weight drop.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to swing the weight up.
Twisting the hips to help move the weight.
benefits: Addresses left-right strength imbalances.
Strong isolated quad contraction.
safetyNotes: Adjust the seat and pad position correctly before loading.
Avoid excessive weight that strains the knee joint.
startingPosition: Knee bent, pad against the shin.
endingPosition: Leg fully extended.

name: Terminal Knee Extension (Band)
instructions: Anchor a resistance band at knee height and loop it behind one knee, standing facing away from the anchor.
Slightly bend the knee, then straighten it fully against the band tension while shifting weight onto that leg.
Return with control to the slightly bent starting position.

instructions: Kneel on a padded surface with your torso upright and hips extended.

instructions: Lean your back against a wall and slide down until your thighs are roughly parallel to the floor.

name: Banded Squat
instructions: Stand on the middle of a resistance band, holding the ends at shoulder height or looped over the shoulders.

instructions: Stand facing a plyometric box a comfortable distance away.

instructions: Attach an ankle cuff to a low cable pulley and secure it around one ankle, facing the machine.

instructions: Kneel with your ankles secured under a pad or held by a partner, torso upright.

instructions: Lie on your back with heels resting on sliders or a towel on a smooth floor, hips lifted.

instructions: Attach an ankle cuff to a low cable pulley and secure it around one ankle, facing the machine.

Return with control, then complete reps before switching sides.

name: Banded Glute Kickback
instructions: Loop a resistance band around one ankle and anchor the other end low in front of you, on all fours or standing.
Kick the banded leg back and up by extending the hip.
Return with control, then complete reps before switching sides.

name: Donkey Kick
instructions: Start on all fours with hands under the shoulders and knees under the hips.
Keeping the knee bent at 90 degrees, kick one foot up toward the ceiling by extending the hip.
Lower with control back to the starting position, then repeat or switch sides.
coachNote: A simple, no-equipment glute isolation exercise popular for high-rep burnout sets.

name: Fire Hydrant
instructions: Start on all fours with hands under the shoulders and knees under the hips.
Keeping the knee bent, raise one leg out to the side until the thigh is roughly parallel to the floor.
Lower with control back to the starting position, then repeat or switch sides.
coachNote: This targets the glute medius and minimus, the often-underdeveloped side glute muscles important for hip stability.

name: Reverse Hyperextension
instructions: Lie face down on the reverse hyperextension machine with your hips at the edge of the pad, legs hanging below.
Swing your legs up by extending the hips until they're roughly in line with your torso.
Lower with control back to the starting position.

name: Sumo Squat (Dumbbell/Kettlebell)
instructions: Stand with a wide stance, toes pointed outward, holding a dumbbell or kettlebell with both hands between your legs.
Squat down by bending the hips and knees, pushing the knees out in line with the toes.

Keep the back flat throughout.
startingPosition: Wide stance, toes out, weight held between the legs.
endingPosition: Thighs at or below parallel, then returned to standing.

name: Curtsy Lunge
instructions: Stand holding dumbbells at your sides.
Step one leg diagonally behind and across the other, lowering into a curtsy-like lunge.
Drive through the front leg to return to standing, then repeat or switch sides.

name: Lateral Lunge
instructions: Stand holding dumbbells at your sides.
Step one leg out to the side and lower into a squat on that leg while keeping the other leg straight.
Drive through the bent leg to return to standing, then repeat or switch sides.
coachNote: Training in the frontal (side-to-side) plane is a valuable addition to a program dominated by forward-backward movements.

name: Lateral Step-Up
instructions: Stand sideways next to a box or bench, holding dumbbells at your sides.
Step up sideways onto the box with the near foot, driving through that leg.
Step back down with control and repeat, or switch sides.
coachNote: The lateral stepping pattern emphasizes the glute medius more than a standard forward step-up.
tips: Drive through the working leg on the box.
Keep the torso upright throughout.
commonMistakes: Using momentum from the trailing leg.

Choose a height that allows a controlled step.
startingPosition: Standing sideways next to the box, dumbbells at the sides.

name: Step-Down (Eccentric, Glute Focus)
instructions: Stand on a box or step with one foot, the other leg hanging off the edge.
Slowly lower the hanging leg toward the floor by bending the standing leg, controlling the descent.
Lightly tap the floor or hover just above it, then drive back up to standing on the box.

Start with a lower step height while learning control.
startingPosition: Standing on the box, one leg hanging off the edge.
endingPosition: Hanging leg lowered near the floor, standing leg bent.

name: Banded Lateral Walk
instructions: Place a resistance band around your legs, just above or below the knees, and assume a quarter-squat stance.
Step sideways with control, maintaining tension on the band throughout.
Continue for the desired distance or reps, then repeat in the opposite direction.
coachNote: A staple warm-up exercise for activating the glute medius before squats or lower-body training.

Stay low in the quarter-squat position throughout.

Letting the feet drift together, losing band tension.

Simple, portable warm-up tool.
safetyNotes: Check the band for wear before use.
Keep the knees tracking over the toes.
startingPosition: Quarter-squat stance, band around the legs.
endingPosition: Same stance, stepped sideways with band tension maintained.

name: Monster Walk (Band)
instructions: Place a resistance band around your legs, just above the knees, and assume a quarter-squat stance.
Step forward diagonally with control, maintaining tension on the band throughout.
Continue for the desired distance, then repeat walking backward.
coachNote: The diagonal, forward-walking pattern adds a multi-planar hip and glute activation challenge compared to a straight lateral walk.

Popular warm-up for athletic and field-sport training.

Keep the knees tracking over the toes.
startingPosition: Quarter-squat stance, band around the legs.
endingPosition: Same stance, stepped diagonally forward with band tension maintained.

name: Standing Cable Hip Extension
instructions: Attach an ankle cuff to a low cable pulley and secure it around one ankle, facing the machine with a slight forward lean.
Extend the leg straight back by squeezing the glute, keeping the knee mostly straight.
Return with control, then complete reps before switching sides.

name: Dumbbell Good Morning
instructions: Hold a dumbbell against your chest or a pair at your sides, standing tall.
Hinge forward at the hips with a soft knee bend, keeping the back flat.
Return to standing by driving the hips forward.

name: Elevated Glute Bridge (Feet on Bench)
instructions: Lie on your back with your heels resting on a bench, knees bent.
Drive through your heels to raise your hips until your body forms a straight line.

name: Kickstand Romanian Deadlift
instructions: Stand holding dumbbells with most of your weight on one foot, the other foot's toes lightly touching the floor behind you for balance (kickstand position).
Hinge forward at the hips, lowering the dumbbells along your legs.
Drive the hips forward to return to standing, then switch sides.

Accessible entry point into unilateral hinging.

name: Barbell Glute Bridge
instructions: Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent and feet flat, a padded barbell rolled over your hips.
Drive through your heels to raise your hips until your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees.
Squeeze the glutes at the top, then lower with control.

name: Machine Hip Adduction
instructions: Sit in the hip adduction machine with the pads positioned against the inside of your knees, legs spread.
Squeeze your legs together against the pads.

instructions: Sit in the hip abduction machine with the pads against the outside of your knees, legs together.
Push your legs outward against the pads.

Pull the leg across your body, adducting the hip.

Raise the leg out to the side, abducting the hip.

name: Copenhagen Plank
instructions: Lie on your side with the top foot resting on a bench, supporting your body on your forearm.
Raise your hips off the floor into a side plank position, holding the position for a set duration.

instructions: Lie on your side with the bottom leg straight and the top leg crossed over, foot flat on the floor in front.
Raise the bottom leg up toward the ceiling by squeezing the inner thigh.
Lower with control back to the starting position, then complete reps before switching sides.

Direct adductor isolation.

Raise the top leg up toward the ceiling, keeping it straight.

instructions: Lie on your side with knees bent roughly 90 degrees and a resistance band looped around your thighs, feet together.
Keeping your feet together, raise the top knee up against the band resistance.
Lower with control back to the starting position, then complete reps before switching sides.

name: Cossack Squat
instructions: Stand with a wide stance, holding a kettlebell at your chest.
Shift your weight to one side, bending that knee into a deep squat while keeping the other leg straight, foot flat.
Push back through the bent leg to return to the centered starting position, then repeat on the other side.

name: Sumo Squat Pulse (Adductor Focus)
instructions: Stand in a wide sumo stance, toes pointed outward, and squat down to a comfortable depth.

name: Standing Banded Adduction Squeeze
instructions: Place a small resistance ball or folded pad between your knees while standing.
Squeeze your knees together against the ball or pad as hard as possible.
Hold for the desired duration, then release with control.
coachNote: A simple isometric adductor strengthening exercise commonly used in groin injury rehab programs.

instructions: Place a resistance band around your ankles and assume a shoulder-width stance with a slight knee bend.
Step sideways with control, keeping tension on the band throughout.

name: Seated Calf Raise (Machine)
instructions: Sit in the machine with the pad resting on your knees and the balls of your feet on the platform.
Lower your heels below the platform to stretch the calves.
Rise up onto your toes as high as possible, squeezing the calves at the top.

instructions: Stand with a barbell racked across your upper back, balls of your feet on a raised surface such as a plate.
Lower your heels toward the floor to stretch the calves.
Rise up onto your toes as high as possible, squeezing the calves at the top.

name: Standing Dumbbell Calf Raise

Lower your heels toward the floor to stretch the calves.
Rise up onto your toes as high as possible, squeezing the calves at the top.

Lower your heel toward the floor to stretch the calf.

instructions: Stand on one foot holding a dumbbell in the same-side hand, balls of your foot on a raised surface, other hand on a support.
Lower your heel toward the floor to stretch the calf.
Rise up onto your toes as high as possible, then repeat before switching sides.

name: Donkey Calf Raise
instructions: Position yourself in the donkey calf raise machine, bent forward at the hips with the pad across your lower back and balls of your feet on the platform.
Lower your heels below the platform to stretch the calves.
Rise up onto your toes as high as possible, squeezing the calves at the top.
coachNote: The bent-over position changes the angle of pull on the calves slightly compared to a standing calf raise, adding useful training variety.

name: Tibialis Raise
instructions: Stand with your back against a wall, heels a few inches away from it.
Raise your toes and the front of your feet up toward your shins as high as possible, keeping the heels planted.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Training the tibialis anterior — the muscle on the front of the shin — balances out heavy calf training and supports ankle and shin health.
